title: Molten Aluminum-Induced Corrosion and Wear-Resistance Properties of ZrB<sub>2</sub>-Based Cermets Improved by Sintering-Temperature Manipulation.

recollection.starting_material: Guess: ZrB2-based cermet powder, probably containing secondary metallic binders (e.g., Ni, Co) and/or ceramic reinforcements such as SiC or TiB2.
recollection.intervention: Guess: Hot-press or spark-plasma sintering at several temperatures (perhaps 1600–2000 °C) to study how higher sintering temperature changes microstructure and properties; subsequent exposure to molten Al and wear testing.
recollection.structure: Guess: Higher sintering temperatures produced a denser, finer-grained ZrB2 matrix with reduced porosity and better distribution of the binder/reinforcement phases; after Al attack, a thin protective layer (Al2O3/ZrO2/boride complex) formed on the surface.
recollection.mechanism: Guess: Improved densification and elimination of open porosity limited molten-Al penetration; reaction products at the interface formed a continuous, adherent barrier layer that suppressed further corrosion and also boosted hardness/wear resistance.
recollection.results: Guess: Corrosion mass-loss in molten Al dropped by a factor of ~3–5 at the optimum sintering temperature; wear rate decreased by ~40–60 %, and hardness and fracture toughness rose (e.g., Vickers hardness to ~18–20 GPa, KIC to ~4–5 MPa·m½).

score.note: The intervention identifies multi-temperature SPS/hot pressing plus molten-Al and wear testing, but the proposed temperature range is inaccurate and no correct optimum is given. The densification/porosity structural trend and pore-blocking mechanism are directionally correct, while the finer-grain claim and protective oxide/boride barrier are unsupported. Quantitatively, the estimated hardness (~18–20 GPa) is close to 1911.8 HV (~18.75 GPa), and the corrosion improvement factor overlaps the actual roughly 2–4× range, though toughness is underestimated and the wear reduction is not tied to the reported 0.104 mm³.
